How to read the ladder

  1. 0 Proposed An idea with a reasoned argument, but no direct patient data yet.
  2. 1 First signs One or more small or uncontrolled studies point towards it.
  3. 2 Backed in a defined group A in patients with a recognised supports it.
  4. 3 Repeated by others An independent group has reproduced the finding in a separate .
  5. 4 Tested by intervention Changing the proposed factor changes the outcome in a controlled experiment, so the link goes beyond association.
  6. 5 Causal case built Several independent lines of evidence, including experimental evidence, together meet most of the , with no unresolved major contradiction.

Each bar shows causal evidence on this six-step . Hypotheses are sorted by furthest along, not by an editorial opinion. The ladder is a draft, pending expert review.

are not mutually exclusive. They may be links in one chain, or may apply to different groups of patients.

Explanations of the marked words on this page

Myalgic encephalomyelitis / chronic fatigue syndrome. Severe fatigue that is worse after effort, with unrefreshing sleep. Older papers say CFS or ME; the names came with different case definitions.
Marked when a study of comparable or higher quality contradicts the finding behind a rung. The founder decides. The disputed rung is drawn hatched on the bar.
Post-exertional malaise. Symptoms get worse after physical or mental effort that was manageable before. It often starts hours to a day or more later and can last days or longer.
Health problems that continue or start after a COVID-19 infection and last at least three months. Some of its symptoms overlap with those of ME/CFS.
People who are compared with the patients, usually healthy people, to see whether a difference is linked to the illness. A study with such a group is called controlled.
A written set of rules (symptoms, how long they have lasted, and illnesses that must be ruled out) used to decide who counts as having ME/CFS in a study.
A group of people followed or studied together.
Nine considerations from 1965 for judging whether a link between two things is likely to be causal, such as strength, consistency and whether the cause comes first.
The six-step scale this site uses to show how much evidence supports a hypothesis, from "Proposed" to "Causal case built". It is a draft.
A hypothesis is a proposed explanation that has not been settled. Here, an idea about what causes ME/CFS.
